title: Cryobank Operations (Awareness Level)
desc: Understand how biological sample banks are run: consent, labelling, cold storage, records, security and ethics. Awareness only.
outcomes: Explain what a cryobank stores and why consent matters.
Fill a sample record and label correctly.
Find risks in the cold chain.
Judge a bank's policies for security and fairness.
task: Create a daily operations checklist and a sample record template for a practice cryobank, and run a mock audit.
condition: A computer, practice forms and a mentor. No real samples, personal data or hazardous materials are used.
standard: Checklist covers temperature, alarms, labelling, access and records; mock audit finds at least 3 planted errors; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Lab trainees, hospital store staff, health administrators.
evidence: checklist, record template, mock audit report
modules: What a cryobank holds
Understand
A cryobank stores biological samples at very low temperatures so they can be used later under agreed conditions.
Samples include cells, tissue, cord blood, reproductive cells and research samples.
Very low temperatures slow biological activity almost to a stop.
Each sample has an owner or custodian, a purpose and conditions of use.
A bank must be able to find, protect and prove the identity of every sample.
A family stores cord blood. The contract states storage period, who may request release, fees and what happens if the bank closes.
Summarise in one paragraph what a cryobank stores, why consent matters and how a sample is found again.
Summary names consent, storage conditions and traceability.
Consent and ownership
Understand
People must understand what they agree to, and they must be able to change their mind within the rules.
Consent in plain language: purpose, duration, research use, fees, risks and withdrawal.
Children's samples need guardian consent and a plan for when the child becomes an adult.
Rules for disposal and for research use must be stated.
Keep signed forms linked to the sample record.
A form has a research-use tick box that defaults to "No". The donor ticks "Yes, anonymised only" and signs. The ID on the form matches the sample label.
Review a sample consent form and list four gaps.
Four real gaps found with a suggested fix for each.
Labelling and records
Apply
A sample without a correct label is a lost sample.
Unique ID, date, sample type, volume, location (tank, rack, box, slot).
Two-person check at entry and removal.
Barcode plus a paper backup.
Never reuse or overwrite an ID.
Sample C-2031 is logged in tank 2, rack B, box 4, slot 7 by Ana and verified by Ravi. The barcode scan matches the form before the sample moves.
Fill five practice records and swap with a peer to check.
No errors and each record has two initials.
Cold chain and alarms
Analyse
Temperature is the main risk. A failure can destroy samples in hours.
Daily log of temperature and nitrogen or power levels.
Alarms with a call-out list and backup power.
Transport in validated containers with a logger.
Test alarms regularly.
A night alarm triggers a call at 2:10 am, a technician arrives within 20 minutes and refills the tank before the temperature rises.
Mark five cold-chain risks on a floor plan and write a control for each.
Every risk has a control and an owner.
Safety for staff
Apply
Extreme cold and nitrogen create real hazards.
Wear cryogenic gloves, face shield and apron when handling.
Oxygen sensors in rooms with nitrogen; ventilation.
Never work alone; know the evacuation route.
First aid for cold burns.
The oxygen alarm sounds. Staff leave the room immediately, ventilate from outside and only re-enter when the reading is safe.
Write five safety rules and one emergency drill.
Rules are specific and the drill names who does what.
Security and privacy
Evaluate
Access is limited and logged because the data and samples are sensitive.
Badge access, camera at doors and a visitor log.
Only authorised staff see identity data.
Data stored securely and deleted per the rule.
Report breaches quickly.
A visitor must show ID, sign the log and be escorted. The log shows time in and out.
Review a security policy and list three strengths and three gaps.
Strengths and gaps are specific.
Ethics, fairness and cost
Evaluate
Banks must be honest about benefits, fees and risks.
Clear fees and no pressure.
No misleading claims about future cures.
An exit plan if the bank closes.
Respect differing cultural and faith views.
A bank publishes a plan to transfer samples to another licensed bank at no extra charge if it closes.
List five ethics questions you would ask a bank.
Questions are fair and specific.
Checklist and mock audit
Create
Practice the routine and prove you can find faults.
Daily, weekly and monthly checklist.
Audit trail and corrective action.
Plant three errors for a peer to find.
Review monthly.
A mock audit finds a missing second-person check, a late temperature entry and an unlabelled box. Each gets a corrective action.
Run a mock audit and write the report.
At least three planted errors found and fixed.
quiz: What does a cryobank store?
Cells, tissue or cord blood at low temperatures. (Covered in module 1: What a cryobank holds. To pass that module: Summary names consent, storage conditions and traceability.)
Why two-person checks?
They catch labelling mistakes. (Covered in module 2: Consent and ownership. To pass that module: Four real gaps found with a suggested fix for each.)
Name a cold-chain risk.
Power failure or low nitrogen. (Covered in module 3: Labelling and records. To pass that module: No errors and each record has two initials.)
Name a safety rule.
Never work alone; use ventilation. (Covered in module 4: Cold chain and alarms. To pass that module: Every risk has a control and an owner.)
Who may access data?
Authorised staff only. (Covered in module 5: Safety for staff. To pass that module: Rules are specific and the drill names who does what.)
What does consent include?
Use, duration, research, right to withdraw. (Covered in module 6: Security and privacy. To pass that module: Strengths and gaps are specific.)
Why backup labels?
Barcodes can fail. (Covered in module 7: Ethics, fairness and cost. To pass that module: Questions are fair and specific.)
What is an exit plan?
Steps to move samples if the bank closes. (Covered in module 8: Checklist and mock audit. To pass that module: At least three planted errors found and fixed.)
What is an audit trail?
Records showing who did what and when. (Covered in module 8: Checklist and mock audit. To pass that module: At least three planted errors found and fixed.)
Why logs?
To show control and find faults. (Covered in module 8: Checklist and mock audit. To pass that module: At least three planted errors found and fixed.)

Checked, dated and explained to others
